title: Do not keep it all in one basket
body:
Concentration risk means too much of your money depends on one borrower, lender or issuer. If that one party delays a payment, a large part of your money is stuck at the same time. Spreading money across several independent places limits how much any single problem can hurt.

Example: you have 10 lakh rupees to place. You put 8 lakh with one borrower, and its payouts are delayed by a year. So 80 percent of your money waits. If you had put 2 lakh each with five unrelated borrowers, one delay would hold up only 20 percent, which is 2 lakh. The other 8 lakh keeps working as planned.

Spreading does not remove risk, and it can add effort and costs. But it is a simple way to avoid a single point of failure.

What to check: What share of your total money sits with any one borrower, lender or issuer?

Education, not investment advice.

title: Keep a paper trail
body:
Money that lives in an app, a chat or a handshake is hard to prove later. If a payment stops or a dispute starts, records are what you can show. A few minutes of filing at the start saves a lot of trouble.

Example: you lend 50,000 rupees for 12 months at 10 percent a year, paid as one amount at the end. Keep the written terms, proof of the transfer, the maturity date and the contact details. At the end you should receive 55,000 rupees, which is 50,000 plus 5,000 interest. If only 52,000 arrives, your records show exactly what was agreed and what is missing.

Update your records whenever a payout arrives. Note the date and the amount, not only the total.

What to check: Can you find the terms, the proof of payment and the maturity date in one place in under a minute?

Education, not investment advice.

title: A price rise is not yet your profit
body:
An asset can show a higher value on paper, but that gain is only real once you sell and the money reaches you. Selling can cost something: fees, making charges, taxes or a lower price than the one you see on screen. The number that matters is what you keep.

Example: you buy an asset for 5 lakh rupees, and it now looks worth 5.6 lakh. On paper your gain is 60,000 rupees. Suppose selling costs 3 percent of the sale value. That is 16,800 rupees, so you receive 5,43,200 rupees. Your real gain is 43,200 rupees, about a quarter smaller than the paper gain.

Tax may also apply. The rules change, so check the current rules.

What to check: What would you actually receive after every cost of selling today, not the price on the screen?

Education, not investment advice.
